title: Josefa Cabezas
text:
Hi! I am an applied researcher interested in how simple, behaviorally informed interventions can reduce inequality in education.
My background combines field experiments, data work, model development, and research communication. My master’s thesis studied behavioral barriers preventing women from undergoing mammography screening, and I currently work at ETH Zurich supporting data, modelling, and tool development in a research group.
I am especially interested in experimental economics, economics of education, parental involvement, educational transitions, and interventions that help research travel into practice.
I strongly believe in clear and simple research communication for a better future.
This website collects my CV, research projects, academic and professional trajectory, and occasional reflections on topics I like and am interested in.

title: Research Projects
text:
Collaborators: D. Schwartz and S. Mondschein
This project studies whether behavioral nudges can increase participation in breast cancer screening programs. Using a field experiment, we evaluate how different communication strategies affect patient engagement and follow-through.
Status: Work in progress.

This project examines how humanized AI avatars and messenger characteristics influence patients’ adherence to post-procedure instructions. The study consists of two randomized experiments focused on communication effectiveness in healthcare contexts.
Status: Accepted at JMIR.

section: Identifying Factors Predicting Kidney Graft Survival in Chile Using Elastic-Net-Regularized Cox Regression
text:
Identifying Factors Predicting Kidney Graft Survival in Chile Using Elastic-Net-Regularized Cox Regression
With: L. Magga, S. Maturana, M. Olivares, M. Valdevenito, J. Chapochnik, F. González, A. Kompatzki, H. Müller, J. Pefaur, C. Ulloa, and R. Valjalo
Published in Medicina (2022).
This paper develops predictive models for kidney graft survival using regularized survival analysis techniques applied to Chilean transplant data.

title: Trajectories
text:
Forest Studio
At ETH Zürich, I currently contribute to the development of Forest Studio, a forest dynamics model designed both for teaching and for practical forestry applications.
The model simulates forest development at the tree level, incorporating modules for growth, mortality, regeneration, thinning, and clear-cut management. One of its distinguishing features is its focus on individual trees rather than aggregated tree groups, allowing for more flexible and detailed management analysis.
A central focus of the project is the management component — particularly thinning strategies — which aims to make the model useful not only as an educational tool, but also as a practical decision-support system for forestry practitioners.
My work involves model development, data analysis, and the translation of complex modeling concepts into tools that are both technically robust and usable in practice.


Other Directions
My broader interests lie in the intersection of: - applied modeling, - human behavior, - decision-making, - and communication of complex systems.
